extracted.intended_audience: readers of political economy: economists, policymakers, merchants, and informed public
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts principles and policy criteria about what determines wages, profits, and inequalities among employments of labour and stock, and evaluates institutional effects (corporations, apprenticeships, market extent) on those outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreeableness or disagreeableness of the business
rubrics_metrics.description: “The agreeableness or disagreeableness of the business” is one of the circumstances which vary the wages of labour and (to a lesser extent) affect the profits of stock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More disagreeable employments command higher pecuniary wages; this characteristic affects labour much more than stock. The ordinary profit of stock rises with risk but not always in proportion to disagreeableness. (Original wording emphasises this as one of five circumstances that vary wages.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk or security with which an employment is attended
rubrics_metrics.description: Risk or security of the trade influences the ordinary rate of profit: riskier trades tend to yield higher profits, though not necessarily in proportion to the risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bankruptcies are more frequent in hazardous trades (e.g., smuggling yields high returns when successful but leads to frequent ruin). To fully compensate risk, common returns should both cover occasional losses and provide an insurer-like surplus; competition often prevents such full compensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish wages from profit (apparent profit may be wages disguised)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent high profits in some trades (e.g., apothecaries, small grocers) are frequently the reasonable wages of skilled or trusted labour disguised as profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating profits, account for the labour, skill, trust, and managerial tasks that are effectively being remunerated out of gross returns (examples: apothecary’s drug markups, grocer’s multi-tasking and small-market skill). Deduct a reasonable wage for the proprietor’s labour to reveal the true profit of stock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of market extent on apparent profit and prime cost
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent of the market affects both apparent profit (diminishes it by employing larger stocks) and prime cost (may increase it when supplies must come from greater distances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In large towns retail goods can be cheaper because the same prime cost but lower apparent profit (due to scale) — e.g., grocery goods cheaper in the capital than in small towns; for goods like bread and meat, increased prime cost from distance can offset diminished profit, making prices similar across regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to extend trade with increasing stock fosters accumulation
rubrics_metrics.description: In great towns trade can be extended as stock increases, enabling profits and annual accumulation to grow with the extent of trade and credit; this is why great fortunes more often arise in capitals than in small towns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In small markets, even high percentage profits yield limited absolute returns because capital cannot be profitably enlarged; in large markets, extension of trade permits large absolute accumulations over time (usually via long life of industry, frugality, and attention rather than sudden gains).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and limits of speculative trade vs established trade
rubrics_metrics.description: Speculative merchants enter and quit branches of trade according to expected abnormal profits; their gains and losses do not conform to regular proportions of any established branch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speculation (e.g., switching between corn, wine, sugar trade) is feasible only in places of extensive commerce and correspondence where required intelligence exists. It can yield sudden fortunes or sudden losses and is characteristic of large towns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requisite 1 for equality of advantages: employments well known and long established
rubrics_metrics.description: Equality in the whole advantages and disadvantages of different employments requires that employments be well known and long established in the neighbourhood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New manufactures or branches often pay higher initial wages to attract workers; fashions-based manufactures are unstable and pay more than necessity-based ones. Example: wages higher in places focusing on fashionable manufactures (Birmingham) than in those on long-established necessities (Sheffield).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requisite 2 for equality: employments in ordinary or natural state
rubrics_metrics.description: Equality also requires that employments be in their ordinary or natural state; temporary fluctuations in demand or supply disturb this equality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seasonal demands (harvest, hay-time) or wartime drafts can raise wages temporarily; conversely, decaying manufactures lower wages. Profits of stock fluctuate with commodity prices — those produced by human industry with stable annual output have steadier prices; agricultural goods fluctuate more, inviting speculative operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requisite 3 for equality: employments must be the sole or principal occupations
rubrics_metrics.description: Equality requires that occupations be the sole or principal employment of those who occupy them; when people supplement another occupation, they may accept lower wages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where work is secondary to other subsistence (e.g., cottars in Scotland), labourers may take lower recompense; such double-employment depresses market prices for those products (examples: stockings and spinning in Scotland were produced cheaply as secondary work).

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy-induced inequalities: restraining competition via exclusive privileges
rubrics_metrics.description: Government or corporate policy creates inequalities by restraining competition in some employments — principal means are exclusive privileges of corporations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corporation privileges restrict entry to those 'free of the trade' (often requiring local apprenticeship). Bye-laws can limit number of apprentices or length of apprenticeship to limit competition (examples: Sheffield master cutlers limited to one apprentice; hatters limited to two apprentices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apprenticeship regulation as a mechanism to restrict competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation of apprenticeships (length and number allowed per master) is used to limit the number who can enter a trade, thereby restraining competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limiting apprentices directly restricts future practitioners; long apprenticeship terms raise the expense of education and indirectly constrain entry. These measures reduce competition and help maintain higher prices and profits for incumbents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute of Apprenticeship (5th of Elizabeth) and its operational limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The 5th of Elizabeth required seven years apprenticeship to exercise trades then exercised in England, but judicial interpretation limited its scope to market towns and to trades established before its enactment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of these limits, many later manufactures (e.g., Manchester, Birmingham industries) are not within the statute; legal distinctions create inconsistent and, Smith suggests, foolish rules (e.g., coach-maker vs wheel-wright examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Long apprenticeships do not secure workmanship or prevent fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: Lengthy apprenticeships give no guarantee against poor workmanship, which is more often the effect of fraud than inability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consumer protections like marks and stamps (e.g., sterling mark on plate, stamps on linen and woollen cloth) provide greater security to purchasers than statutes requiring long apprenticeships. Buyers look for marks more than apprenticeship records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long apprenticeships reduce incentive and formation of industry in apprentices
rubrics_metrics.description: Prolonged apprenticeship terms discourage industrious habits: apprentices receive no immediate benefit and tend to be idle; being paid as journeymen by piece-work promotes industriousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Piece-rate employment rewards immediate exertion and promotes early habit of industry. Long binding terms (especially for charity-bound apprentices) often produce idle and worthless workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporations’ regulation to prevent market overstocking (monopolistic intent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporations enact regulations to prevent the market from being 'overstocked' with their own industry, effectively keeping supply limited to sustain higher prices and profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within the town, classes may accept higher internal costs because they can sell more dearly to the country (the town’s dealings with the country are where the advantage and enrichment are realized). Thus, corporate restrictions redistribute benefits in favor of local producers at the expense of outsiders/consumers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy of Europe causes inequalities in three ways
rubrics_metrics.description: European policy produces important inequalities by (1) restraining competition in some employments, (2) increasing it in others beyond natural levels, and (3) obstructing free circulation of labour and stock between employments and places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three channels are the principal mechanisms by which government policy — through corporations, statutes, and other restrictions — distorts the natural leveling forces of free competition and mobility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obstruction of free circulation of labour and stock
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies that hinder labour and stock moving from employment to employment or place to place cause inequalities in advantages and disadvantages across employments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where mobility is restricted, wages and profits cannot adjust to offset non-pecuniary advantages/disadvantages, preventing the leveling that would otherwise occur under perfect freedom.
